questions.question_text: The conductivity of centimolar solution of KCl at $298$ K is $0.021\text{Ohm}^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$ and the resistance of the cell containing the solution at $298$ K is $60\Omega$ . The value of cell constant ( $G^{∗}$ ) is __________.
questions.question_html: The conductivity of centimolar solution of KCl at $298$ K is $0.021\text{Ohm}^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$ and the resistance of the cell containing the solution at $298$ K is $60\Omega$ . The value of cell constant ( $G^{∗}$ ) is __________.
questions.explanation_text: Conductivity is related to conductance and cell constant by $\kappa=G \times G^{∗}$ where $G=\frac{1}{R}$ So, $\kappa=\frac{1}{R} \times G^{∗}$ This gives $G^{∗}=\kappa \times R$ Given, $\kappa=0.021\text{Ohm}^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}$ and $R=60\Omega$ So, $G^{∗}=0.021 \times 60$ $G^{∗}=1.26\text{cm}^{-1}$ So, the correct option is $1.26\text{cm}^{-1}$ Option B.

The other part of $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is getting oxidised to $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ : $2\text{Mn}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{3+}+2e^{-}$ This is the reverse of $2(\text{Mn}^{3+}+e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+})E^{0}=+1.51\text{V}$ So the oxidation potential will be $E_{\text{ox}}^{0}=-1.51\text{V}$ Now, $E_{\text{cell}}^{0}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{0}+E_{\text{anode oxidation}}^{0}$ $E_{\text{cell}}^{0}=(-1.18)+(-1.51)$ $E_{\text{cell}}^{0}=-2.69\text{V}$ Since $E_{\text{cell}}^{0}$ is negative, the reaction is non-spontaneous. one part of $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is getting reduced to $\text{Mn}$ :

The other part of $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is getting oxidised to $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ :

$2\text{Mn}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{3+}+2e^{-}$

This is the reverse of

$2(\text{Mn}^{3+}+e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+})E^{0}=+1.51\text{V}$

So the oxidation potential will be

$E_{\text{ox}}^{0}=-1.51\text{V}$

$E_{\text{cell}}^{0}=E_{\text{cathode}}^{0}+E_{\text{anode oxidation}}^{0}$

$E_{\text{cell}}^{0}=(-1.18)+(-1.51)$

$E_{\text{cell}}^{0}=-2.69\text{V}$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option A:}-2.69\text{V, the reaction will not occur (Non-Spontaneous)}$

questions.question_text: $\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH})}^{0}$ is equal to ____
questions.question_html: $\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH})}^{0}$ is equal to ____
questions.explanation_text: For $\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH}$ , $\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH})}^{0}=\lambda_{\text{NH}_{4}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{0}$ Using Kohlrausch’s law, we combine strong electrolytes whose ions can give $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ . Now, $\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl})}^{0}=\lambda_{\text{NH}_{4}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0}$ $\Lambda_{m(\text{NaOH})}^{0}=\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{0}$ $\Lambda_{m(\text{NaCl})}^{0}=\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0}$ So, $\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl})}^{0}+\Lambda_{m(\text{NaOH})}^{0}-\Lambda_{m(\text{NaCl})}^{0}$ $=(\lambda_{\text{NH}_{4}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0})+(\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{0})-(\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0})$ The $\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}$ and $\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0}$ terms cancel out. $=\lambda_{\text{NH}_{4}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{0}$ $=\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH})}^{0}$ So the correct option is: $\text{Option B}$ $\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl})}^{0}+\Lambda_{m(\text{NaOH})}^{0}-\Lambda_{m(\text{NaCl})}^{0}$
questions.explanation_html:
For $\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH}$ ,

$\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH})}^{0}=\lambda_{\text{NH}_{4}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{0}$

Using Kohlrausch’s law, we combine strong electrolytes whose ions can give $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ .

Now,

$\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl})}^{0}=\lambda_{\text{NH}_{4}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0}$

$\Lambda_{m(\text{NaOH})}^{0}=\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{0}$

$\Lambda_{m(\text{NaCl})}^{0}=\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0}$

So,

$\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl})}^{0}+\Lambda_{m(\text{NaOH})}^{0}-\Lambda_{m(\text{NaCl})}^{0}$

$=(\lambda_{\text{NH}_{4}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0})+(\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{0})-(\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0})$

The $\lambda_{\text{Na}^{+}}^{0}$ and $\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{0}$ terms cancel out.

$=\lambda_{\text{NH}_{4}^{+}}^{0}+\lambda_{\text{OH}^{-}}^{0}$

$=\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH})}^{0}$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option B}$

$\Lambda_{m(\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl})}^{0}+\Lambda_{m(\text{NaOH})}^{0}-\Lambda_{m(\text{NaCl})}^{0}$

questions.explanation_html:
During electrolysis of acidified water, hydrogen gas is formed at the cathode and oxygen gas is formed at the anode.

The overall reaction is

$2H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow 2H_{2}(g)+O_{2}(g)$

From the equation,

$1\text{mole of}O_{2}\text{gives}2\text{moles of}H_{2}$

Given mass of oxygen gas:

$16\text{g}$

Molar mass of $O_{2}$ is

$32\text{g mol}^{-1}$

$\frac{16}{32}=0.5\text{mol}$

$22.4\text{L}$

So, volume of $H_{2}$ gas liberated is

$1 \times 22.4=22.4\text{L}$

$\text{Option A:}22.4\text{L}$

questions.explanation_text: To convert $NaClO_{3}$ to $NaClO_{4}$ using electric current, the reaction is given by: $NaClO_{3}+H_{2}O \longrightarrow NaClO_{4}+H_{2}$ Here, the oxidation states change from: $NaClO_{3}$ with chlorine at (+5 oxidation state) to $NaClO_{4}$ with chlorine at (+7 oxidation state). This means that for every $NaClO_{3}$ molecule converted to $NaClO_{4}$ , 2 moles of electrons are involved (as two electrons are required to change the oxidation state from +5 to +7). According to the reaction stoichiometry: 2 Faradays of charge are needed to provide 2 moles of electrons. Therefore, when 3 Faradays of charge are passed, the moles of electrons supplied will be: $\text{Moles of electrons}=\frac{3}{2}=1.5$ Hence, 1.5 moles of $NaClO_{4}$ will be formed.
